title: Phishing: Spearphishing Voice
summary: Spearphishing Voice, usually called vishing, uses a telephone call or voice message instead of email to move a person into an action that grants access. The caller impersonates a trusted party such as an internal help desk, a bank, a supplier or a senior colleague, and adds urgency so that the target acts before checking. There is often no attachment at all: the target is talked into opening a link, installing remote support software, reading out a one-time code, or approving a push authentication prompt. Some campaigns begin with a phishing email that asks the target to call a number, which lets the adversary control the whole conversation. Detection is largely procedural and identity based, because the call itself leaves no endpoint telemetry. Useful signals include remote support tools installed shortly after a help desk contact, password resets that follow an inbound call, repeated multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts, and new device enrolments immediately after a call. Defenders therefore pair call metadata from the telephone system with the endpoint and sign-in events that follow it.

beginner.definition: Phishing means tricking a person into helping an attacker, usually through a message. This version uses a phone call or a voice message instead of email. The caller pretends to be someone you trust and asks for access, a code or a permission. Many people know this attack as vishing, which is short for voice phishing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your technical controls cannot see a friendly voice on the telephone. One short call can defeat strong passwords and multi-factor authentication, which is a second proof of who you are. Staff who want to be helpful are the easiest target, and attackers know this well. A single successful call can give an intruder a foothold that takes months to remove.
howItWorks: The attacker studies the company and picks a target, often in finance, human resources or the help desk.
Using a false name and a false caller identity, they call and claim to be a manager, supplier or support engineer.
They create urgency, for example a failed payment or an account that will be locked in ten minutes.
They ask for a small action, such as reading a login code or approving a sign-in prompt on a phone.
Sometimes they ask the target to install remote support software so that they can control the computer directly.
After the call they use the access quietly, and they may call again later to ask for more.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk with one tired receptionist. A caller in a calm, official voice says he is the new duty manager and has locked his keys in an office. He asks her to open the staff door just this once. She wants to help and there is nobody awake to ask, so she opens it. Nothing was broken and no rule was written down as broken. Voice phishing works the same way, by turning your helpfulness into the key.
takeaways: Never read a login code or approve a sign-in prompt for someone who called you.
Verify any urgent request through a number or channel you already know and trust.
Report every suspicious call, even if you did not give anything away, because others will receive it too.

objectives: Explain how voice spearphishing differs from phishing that arrives by email.
Describe the social engineering levers of impersonation and urgency that callers rely on.
List the identity and endpoint events that often follow a successful voice phishing call.
Explain why multi-factor authentication prompts can be abused during a phone call.
Describe how to verify a caller's identity using an independent channel before acting.
